title: Drawing the best line
objectives: Fit a line by minimising the sum of squared residuals.
Explain why residuals are vertical and why we square them.

screens.title: Eight days, one line
screens.prose: Each point is one day: the market's return and a stock's return, both in per cent. The sliders move the line. Each vertical segment shows how far the line misses that day, and the corner adds up the squares of those misses.
screens.question: Slide both until the sum of squared misses is as small as you can make it.

hints.text: Set the slope first, then fine-tune the intercept.
The first and last days moved most. They pull hardest on the line's tilt.
Try a slope of 1.2 and an intercept of 0.1.

feedback.correct: That is as low as the corner goes: 3.06, at slope 1.2 and intercept 0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the number in the corner stops falling whichever way you move.

byKey.flat: Your line is nearly flat, so it misses the big market days badly. Tilt it upwards and watch the corner.
byKey.off: Close, but not the lowest yet. Move one slider at a time and keep each move that lowers the corner.

explain.text: The lowest sum is 3.06, at slope 1.2 and intercept 0.1. Every other line misses some days by more. On this line the stock moves 1.2% for each 1% move in the market.

screens.title: Naming the miss
screens.prose: The line you found is the **fitted line** $\hat y = a + bx$, here $\hat y = 0.1 + 1.2x$. Its height at a day's $x$ is the prediction $\hat y_i$. The miss $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$ is that day's **residual**.

state.caption: The marked day: market up 0.3%, stock down 0.04%

screens.question: What is the residual on the marked day, in per cent?

hints.text: First find the line's height at $x = 0.3$.
The point sits below the line, so its residual is negative.

feedback.correct: $e = -0.04 - 0.46 = -0.5$. The stock did 0.5% worse than the line predicted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the line's prediction for the day, then subtract it from the actual return.

byKey.flipped: You took the prediction minus the actual. A residual is actual minus predicted, so a point below the line has a negative residual.
byKey.prediction: 0.46 is the line's prediction, $0.1 + 1.2 \times 0.3$. Subtract it from the actual return.
byKey.raw: That is the actual return. The residual is how far it sits from the line.

explain.text: The line predicts 0.46% for that day ($0.1 + 1.2 \times 0.3$). The stock returned $-0.04$%, so the residual is $-0.04 - 0.46 = -0.5$. Points below the line have negative residuals, drawn in the other colour.

screens.title: Which way is a miss?
screens.prose: We use the market's return to predict the stock's. When we predict, the market's return is already known. Only the stock's return is in doubt.

state.caption: The marked day: market down 0.2%, stock up 1.36%

screens.question: Which gap is the error of our prediction for the marked day?

options.text: The vertical gap: the stock's actual return minus the line's height at the same market return
The horizontal gap from the point to the line
options.why: That gap changes the market's return, which we already know. It would measure an error in predicting $x$ from $y$.

options.text: The shortest, perpendicular distance from the point to the line
options.why: That mixes an error in $x$ with an error in $y$. Our $x$ is known, so all the error is in $y$.

hints.text: Which of the two returns are we trying to predict?
Hold the market return fixed at $-0.2$% and look straight up and down.

feedback.correct: The miss is in the stock's return, so we measure it straight up or down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which number the line is predicting.

byKey.horizontal: You moved along the market axis. We already know the market's return; the line's job is to predict the stock's.
byKey.perpendicular: You measured the shortest distance, which treats both returns as uncertain. Only the stock's return is.

explain.text: We predict $y$ at a known $x$, so a miss is vertical: $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$. In *Fitting a line by least squares* (Orthogonality and Least Squares) we saw that regressing $x$ on $y$ gives a different line. This day misses by 1.5, the largest residual: the company had news.

screens.title: Let the misses cancel?
screens.prose: A colleague scores a line by the plain sum of its residuals and wants that sum to be 0. The flat line $\hat y = 0.16$ passes their test. The sliders are free, so try other lines.
screens.question: What is wrong with the colleague's rule?

options.text: Many lines score 0: every line through $(\bar x, \bar y) = (0.05, 0.16)$ does. The rule cannot choose.
Nothing. A zero sum means the line misses by nothing on average, so it is as good as yours.
options.why: You trusted the zero sum. Misses above and below cancel: this line's squared misses add to 18.12, against 3.06 for yours.

options.text: Only one line has residuals summing to 0, so the flat line must be the least squares line.
options.why: You assumed a zero sum picks out one line. Set the slope to 2 and the intercept to 0.06: the sum is still 0.

hints.text: Try slope 2 with intercept 0.06, then slope 1 with intercept 0.11. Watch the caption.
The flat line misses the first and last days by about 2% each, in opposite directions.
The sum of residuals is $\sum y_i - na - b\sum x_i$. It is 0 whenever $a + b\bar x = \bar y$.

feedback.correct: Every line through the point of means scores 0, steep or flat.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try two very different lines through $(0.05, 0.16)$ and read the caption each time.

byKey.fine: You trusted the zero sum. Misses above and below cancel: this line's squared misses add to 18.12, against 3.06 for yours.
byKey.unique: You assumed a zero sum picks out one line. Set the slope to 2 and the intercept to 0.06: the sum is still 0.

explain.text: The sum of residuals is $\sum y_i - na - b\sum x_i$, which is 0 whenever $\bar y = a + b\bar x$. So every line through the point of means scores 0, however it tilts. Squaring stops misses of opposite sign cancelling: this slope-2 line still costs 9.75.

screens.title: Absolute misses instead
screens.prose: Another way to stop signs cancelling is to drop them: score a line by its sum of **absolute** residuals, $\sum |e_i|$. The caption shows that score; the corner still shows the squared one. The line starts at least squares.
screens.question: Slide to make the sum of absolute residuals as small as you can.

hints.text: The news day's big miss pulls the least squares line up. Does the absolute score care as much?
Lower the intercept below 0, then adjust the slope.
Try slope 1.3 and intercept $-0.2$.

feedback.correct: That is as low as the caption goes on these sliders, about 3.22.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lower the intercept a step at a time, then nudge the slope, keeping each move that lowers the caption.

byKey.ls: You stayed on the least squares line. Its absolute residuals add to 3.60. Lower the intercept and watch the caption fall.
byKey.off: Not the lowest yet. Lower the intercept a little more, then nudge the slope up.

explain.text: The lowest absolute score, 3.18, belongs to $\hat y = -0.228 + 1.32x$, which passes exactly through two of the days. This is the **least absolute deviations** line, a different line from least squares, which is drawn in ink for comparison. It counts the news day's miss at face value, so that day pulls it up less.

screens.title: Why squares
screens.prose: Least squares picks $a$ and $b$ to make $$S(a, b) = \sum_i (y_i - a - b x_i)^2$$ as small as possible. Squares never cancel. $S$ is a smooth bowl with one lowest point, so calculus can find it. Absolute values have corners, and their best line can fail to be unique.
screens.question: The news day has a residual of 1.5. How many times as much does it add to $S$ as a residual of 0.5?

hints.text: Square each residual.

feedback.correct: $2.25 / 0.25 = 9$: three times the miss costs nine times as much.

byKey.ratio: 3 is the ratio of the misses themselves. Squaring makes it $1.5^2 / 0.5^2 = 2.25 / 0.25$.

explain.text: A miss three times as big costs nine times as much. So least squares works hardest to avoid big misses, which is why the news day lifts the whole line. That helps when big misses matter and hurts when one bad point is noise.

screens.title: The best flat line
screens.prose: Start simple: a flat line $\hat y = a$, with no slope. Its score is $S(a) = \sum_i (y_i - a)^2$, a function of $a$ alone. We find the $a$ that makes it smallest.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $S'(a) = -2\sum_i (y_i - a)$, differentiating each square by the chain rule
$\sum_i (y_i - a) = 0$, because the derivative is 0 at the lowest point
$\sum_i y_i - na = 0$, because $a$ appears once in each of the $n$ terms
$a = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i = \bar y$, dividing both sides by $n$

hints.text: Which line differentiates $S$?
Setting something to 0 needs the derivative first. The flat line's misses are drawn on the plot.
Differentiate, set the derivative to 0, split the sum, then divide by $n$.

feedback.correct: The best flat line is the mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by differentiating $S(a)$, then follow each step from the one before.

byKey.s2: You set the sum to 0 before differentiating. The 0 comes from the derivative at the minimum.
byKey.s3: Splitting the sum comes after setting the derivative to 0.
byKey.s4: Dividing by $n$ needs the sum split first.

explain.text: The best flat line is $\hat y = \bar y = 0.16$, and its score, $\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2 = 18.12$, is the total spread of the stock's returns. Our sloped line cuts that to 3.06. Lesson 3 turns this comparison into $R^2$.

screens.title: Only two days
screens.prose: Suppose we had only two days. The market fell 1% while the stock fell 0.9%; then the market rose 2% while the stock rose 2.7%.
screens.question: Move the line until the sum of squared residuals is exactly 0.

hints.text: Two points always lie on one line.
The slope is the rise over the run between the two points.
The rise is $2.7 - (-0.9) = 3.6$ over a run of 3: slope 1.2. Then the intercept is 0.3.

feedback.correct: Slope 1.2 and intercept 0.3 pass through both points, so both residuals are 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line through both points: the corner reads 0 only there.

byKey.b: The tilt is not right yet. A line through both points rises 3.6 over a run of 3.
byKey.a: The slope is right but the line sits off the points. Move the intercept until the corner reads 0.

explain.text: Two points always fit exactly, so both residuals are 0 and the fit says nothing about noise. Misses can only show up once we have more points than the two unknowns. If instead every day had the same market return, the points would stand in a column and no slope would beat another.

screens.title: A day the market fell
screens.prose: A risk model uses our line, $\hat y = 0.1 + 1.2x$. Its slope is the stock's **beta**: the stock moves 1.2% for each 1% the market moves. The next day the market falls 2.5% and the stock falls 3.6%.
screens.question: What is that day's residual, in per cent?

hints.text: Predict first: put $x = -2.5$ into the line.

feedback.correct: $-3.6 - (-2.9) = -0.7$: the stock fell 0.7% more than the market explains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the prediction at $x = -2.5$, then take actual minus predicted.

byKey.flipped: You took predicted minus actual. The stock fell further than predicted, so the residual is negative.
byKey.prediction: $-2.9$ is the prediction. The residual is the actual return minus it.
byKey.no-intercept: You left out the intercept. The line predicts $0.1 + 1.2 \times (-2.5) = -2.9$, not $-3.0$.

explain.text: The line predicts $0.1 - 3.0 = -2.9$, so the residual is $-0.7$. That part of the fall is specific to the stock: a hedge sized by beta would not have covered it. Level 2 asks how sure we can be of the 1.2 itself.

screens.title: Slippage against size
screens.prose: An execution desk fits slippage, in basis points, against order size, in £ millions, over last month's orders. The least squares line is $\hat y = 1.5 + 0.8x$. One £5m order paid 6.2 bp.
screens.question: What is that order's residual, in basis points?

hints.text: What does the line predict for a £5m order?
The marked order sits above the line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Predict the slippage for £5m, then subtract the prediction from what was paid.

byKey.flipped: You took predicted minus actual. The order paid more than predicted, so its residual is positive.
byKey.prediction: 5.5 bp is what the line predicts. The residual is what was paid minus that.

explain.text: The line predicts $1.5 + 0.8 \times 5 = 5.5$ bp, so the residual is $6.2 - 5.5 = 0.7$ bp. On £5m that is £350 more than a typical order of that size paid. A trader would look at that order's timing and venue.

ideas: A residual is actual minus fitted, $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$, measured vertically because we predict $y$ from $x$.
Least squares picks the line $\hat y = a + bx$ with the smallest sum of squared residuals. Squares cannot cancel, give a smooth bowl, and punish big misses.
The plain sum of residuals is 0 for every line through $(\bar x, \bar y)$. Absolute residuals give a different line, least absolute deviations.

formula.name: Least squares score
formula.note: With only two points $S$ can reach 0; with no spread in $x$ no slope beats another.

summary.trap: A zero sum of residuals does not make a line good: every line through the point of means has one.

quiz.prose: On six days the market returned exactly 0.5% each day, while a stock returned anything from $-1$% to 2%.
quiz.question: What slope does least squares give for the stock against the market?

options.text: There is no single best slope: every line through the centre of the points fits equally well

options.why: You read no spread in $x$ as no slope. The points stand in a column, so tilting the line about their centre changes nothing.

options.text: 1, since a stock moves with its market
options.why: You assumed a beta of 1. These six days give no information about tilt at all.

options.text: A vertical line through the column
options.why: A vertical line is not of the form $\hat y = a + bx$. It predicts no single $y$ for $x = 0.5$.

feedback.correct: With no spread in $x$, every tilt about the centre gives the same residuals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changes in the residuals when you tilt a line about a column of points.

explain.text: Every point has $x = 0.5$, so each residual depends only on the line's height at 0.5. Every line with $a + 0.5b = \bar y$ fits equally well. Least squares needs spread in $x$ to pin down a slope.

quiz.prose: Line A misses four points by 1 each. Line B goes exactly through three of them and misses the fourth by 3.
quiz.question: Which line does least squares prefer, and which does least absolute deviations prefer?

options.text: Least squares prefers A (4 against 9); least absolute deviations prefers B (3 against 4)
Both prefer B, since it hits three points exactly
options.why: You counted the exact hits. Least squares turns the miss of 3 into 9, more than A's total of 4.

options.text: Both prefer A, since its misses are all small
options.why: Absolute deviations adds B's misses as $0 + 0 + 0 + 3 = 3$, less than A's 4.

options.text: Least squares prefers B; least absolute deviations prefers A
options.why: You swapped the two scores. Squares punish B's single big miss: $3^2 = 9$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both scores for both lines.

explain.text: Squared, A scores $4 \times 1^2 = 4$ and B scores $3^2 = 9$, so least squares picks A. In absolute values A scores 4 and B scores 3, so least absolute deviations picks B. Squaring makes one big miss worse than several small ones.

quiz.prose: Three days of a stock's returns: 1%, 2% and 6%. We fit a flat line $\hat y = a$ by least squares.
quiz.question: What is the best $a$, in per cent?

widget.label: Best flat line, in per cent

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Setting the derivative of $\sum (y_i - a)^2$ to 0 gives a familiar average.

byKey.median: 2 is the median, the best flat line for absolute residuals. Squares pick the mean.

explain.text: Setting $S'(a) = -2\sum (y_i - a)$ to 0 gives $a = \bar y = 3$. Its score is $4 + 1 + 9 = 14$. The median, 2, scores $1 + 0 + 16 = 17$, so squares prefer the mean.

quiz.prose: An impact model is $\hat y = 2 + 0.5x$, with impact in bp and size in £m. Orders of £2m, £4m and £6m paid 3.5, 3.6 and 5.4 bp.
quiz.question: What is the sum of squared residuals?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Predict each order, take actual minus predicted, then square and add.

byKey.sum: 0.5 is the plain sum of the residuals. Square each one before adding.
byKey.abs: 1.3 adds the absolute residuals. Square them instead.

explain.text: The line predicts 3, 4 and 5 bp, so the residuals are 0.5, $-0.4$ and 0.4. Their squares are 0.25, 0.16 and 0.16, which add to 0.57. The plain sum, 0.5, would hide the negative miss.
